snip.t: Kidney (glomerulus & tubules): Filtration pressure, sodium handling, tubuloglomerular feedback — Hypertensive nephrosclerosis and secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, glomerulonephritis) alter this feedback, perpetuating hypertension
Renal artery stenosis: Abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary oedema, creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor; Doppler or CT angiography
ACEIs/ARBs: Contraindicated in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, and severe hyperkalaemia.
Contra‑indications / safety: • ACE‑I/ARB in bilateral renal artery stenosis → stop if creatinine rises >30 % — • NSAIDs – avoid; they reduce renal perfusion
ACEI/ARB contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy, or severe hyperkalaemia.

Medication safety – “Why would you stop an ACE inhibitor in a patient with a sudden rise in serum creatinine of 30 %?” (Answer: suspect bilateral renal artery stenosis or acute tubular necrosis; need to reassess).

qs.q: What is the gold standard investigation used to diagnose renal artery stenosis?
o: Renal duplex ultrasonography
Catheter angiography procedure
Plain abdominal X-ray imaging
Urinary cortisol excretion test
qs.e: Intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography (catheter angiography) is the gold standard renal arteriogram used for diagnosing renal artery stenosis. Renal duplex ultrasonography is used as a first-line test rather than the gold standard.

qs.q: A 65-year-old male smoker with diabetes is found to have renovascular hypertension. What is the most common underlying pathological cause of main renal artery stenosis in this patient demographic?
o: Uncontrolled complement activation due to a lack of regulatory proteins
Fibromuscular thickening involving the media and adventitia of the renal artery
Concentric atherosclerotic plaque formation at the origin of the renal artery
Endothelial injury secondary to Shiga-like toxin from bacterial enteritis
qs.e: Atherosclerotic plaque accounts for 70% of renal artery stenosis cases and is more common in older men and diabetics. Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects younger women rather than older male smokers.

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia. How do the internal arterioles of the ischemic kidney typically appear compared to the contralateral kidney?
o: Obstructed by large von Willebrand factor multimers and microthrombi
Exposed to full systemic hypertension, showing severe medial thickening
Completely obliterated by hyaline arteriolosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis
Protected from high pressure, showing only mild arteriolosclerosis
qs.e: The stenosis shields the downstream kidney from full systemic pressure, so its internal arterioles show only mild arteriolosclerosis while the opposite kidney suffers severe changes. The contralateral kidney is the one exposed to the full force of high pressure.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with a history of generalized atherosclerosis and progressive renal failure undergoes renal duplex ultrasonography, which reveals diffuse, bilateral luminal narrowing of the main renal vessels. Which of the following best characterizes this presentation compared to typical unilateral renal artery stenosis?
o: Fibromuscular dysplasia origin
Bilateral and gradual course
Cholesterol crystal deposition
Acute malignant presentation
qs.e: Atherosclerotic ischemic renal disease typically involves bilateral, slowly progressive narrowing leading to chronic renal failure. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a distinct cause of renal artery stenosis that primarily affects younger females rather than causing this bilateral atherosclerotic pattern.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old male presents with newly diagnosed hypertension found to be caused by renal artery stenosis. What percentage of all hypertension cases are attributed to this specific renovascular condition?
o: 25 to 30 percent
10 to 15 percent
2 to 5 percent
40 to 50 percent
qs.e: Renal artery stenosis is responsible for 2 to 5 percent of all hypertension cases and represents a curable cause. Higher percentages incorrectly overestimate the known prevalence of this specific condition.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 35-year-old female is diagnosed with renal artery stenosis resulting from fibromuscular dysplasia. Which demographic and vessel layer feature distinguishes this pathology from atherosclerosis?
o: Cholesterol crystal embolization following catheterization
Concentric calcified plaque in older males
Thrombotic microthrombi caused by Shiga-like toxin
Fibrous thickening of the vessel wall in younger women
qs.e: Fibromuscular dysplasia involves fibrous thickening of the vessel wall and is more common in younger women in their 30s and 40s without atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is characteristically found in older males.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: When examining a kidney affected by chronic unilateral renal artery stenosis, which gross and microscopic finding is typically observed?
o: Enlarged kidney with severe arteriolosclerosis
Wedge-shaped pale infarct with complete arterial blockage
Smaller kidney showing diffuse ischemic atrophy
Normal sized organ with marked hyperperfusion
qs.e: The kidney with renal artery stenosis is smaller than normal and exhibits diffuse ischemic atrophy with crowded glomeruli and interstitial fibrosis. Complete arterial blockage causes a wedge-shaped infarct rather than general ischemic atrophy.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: In a patient with unilateral renal artery stenosis, the two kidneys experience vastly different pressure environments. How do the internal arterioles of the stenotic kidney compare to those of the contralateral kidney?
o: Contralateral kidney arterioles are shielded from systemic pressure by the plaque
Both kidneys exhibit identical degrees of severe malignant arteriolosclerosis
Stenotic kidney arterioles show mild arteriolosclerosis due to pressure protection
Stenotic kidney arterioles experience full high pressure resulting in severe damage
qs.e: The stenosis shields the ipsilateral kidney from high systemic pressure, causing its arterioles to show only mild arteriolosclerosis. The opposite kidney is exposed to full high pressure and develops more severe arteriolosclerosis.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is a narrowing of the renal artery that reduces kidney perfusion, activates the renin‑angiotensin system, and drives resistant hypertension and kidney injury. It is most often caused by atherosclerosis in older men or fibromuscular dysplasia in younger women.

sections.p: RAS is a focal or diffuse narrowing of the renal artery that limits blood flow to the kidney. Diagnosis relies on imaging and functional tests that demonstrate a significant pressure drop across the lesion.
b: Atherosclerotic RAS: >70% luminal narrowing; FMD: string‑of‑beads appearance

t.b: Assesses peak systolic velocity; a velocity >200 cm/s suggests >70% stenosis.
Visualises the artery; a 70% or greater reduction confirms RAS.
High renin in the affected kidney versus contralateral kidney supports functional significance.
Elevated plasma renin and aldosterone with normal potassium indicates secondary hyperaldosteronism due to RAS.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of luminal narrowing and by kidney function. Staging guides treatment urgency.
b: Stage 3: ≥70% stenosis, severe CKD or refractory hypertension

sections.p: The etiology depends on age, sex, and comorbidities. In low‑resource settings, infections and systemic diseases can also contribute.
b: Atherosclerosis – age >55, male, smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia
Fibromuscular dysplasia – young women, often unilateral
Hypertension secondary to chronic kidney disease

sections.p: Patients often have resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary oedema, or a new rise in creatinine after starting ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
b: Unilateral flank pain if severe stenosis

sections.p: Choose tests based on availability and clinical suspicion. When a test is unavailable, use clinical clues and basic labs.

t.b: Detects resistant hypertension; a systolic >180 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg despite therapy.
Rising creatinine after ACEI/ARB suggests RAS.
Proteinuria may indicate kidney damage but is non‑specific.

Gold standard when available; confirms anatomy.
Functional confirmation when imaging is equivocal.

sections.p: RAS can precipitate acute kidney injury, flash pulmonary oedema, and uncontrolled hypertension, which may be fatal if untreated.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control blood pressure, and consider revascularisation in selected patients.
b: Control BP with calcium channel blockers or diuretics first; avoid ACEI/ARB until RAS is ruled out
Consider percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting if >70% stenosis and refractory hypertension or progressive renal failure
Surgical bypass is reserved for complex lesions

Lower volume load; useful in hypertension.

Severe refractory hypertension despite multiple drugs

faq.q: Why does ACEI/ARB worsen kidney function in RAS?
faq.a: They block angiotensin II, which normally constricts the efferent arteriole; without it, glomerular filtration drops when perfusion is already low.
Yes, many patients have no symptoms until a precipitating event like ACEI initiation or severe hypertension.
